THIS MISCELLANEOUS FIRST APPEAL IS FILED UNDER SECTION 173(1) OF MV ACT PRAYING TO SET ASIDE THE JUDGMENT AND AWARD DATED 11.01.2018 PASSED BY THE SENIOR CIVIL JUDGE & MACT, MUDIGERE IN M.V.C.NO.365/2016.

THESE MISCELLANEOUS FIRST APPEALS HAVING BEEN HEARD AND RESERVED ON 30.03.2023 COMING ON FOR PRONOUNCEMENT OF JUDGMENT THIS DAY, K.S.MUDAGAL J.,
DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 JUDGMENT Challenging the award in M.V.C.No.365/2016 on the file of the Senior Civil Judge and MACT,
Mudigere, the claimants have preferred M.F.A.No.1839/2018 and the registered owner and the driver of the insured vehicle have preferred M.F.A.No.2818/2018.
2.
For the purpose of convenience, the parties will be referred to henceforth according to their ranks before the Tribunal.
3. Claimant No.1 is the wife, claimant Nos.2 and 3 are the minor children and claimant No.4 is the mother of the deceased Keerthi @ Vijayakumar (for short 'Keerthi').
On 12.11.2011 the JCB Machine bearing No.JS.81 was being transported in Tipper Lorry bearing registration No.KA-53-5298.
According to the claimants, Keerthi was Operator of the said JCB Machine and on loading the machine in the body of the lorry, he was sitting at the cabin of the JCB Machine.

At 10.30 a.m. when the lorry was proceeding at a place called Ambalapadav within the limits of Karkala Rural Police Station, Keerthi was electrocuted on account of some live wire passing over the road.
He was shifted to Geetha Clinic initially and then to Alva Hospital.
There he was declared brought dead.

At the relevant time, respondent No.1 was the driver, respondent No.2 was the registered owner and respondent No.3 was the insurer of the lorry bearing registration No.KA-53-5298.
4.
Regarding the incident, PW.2 filed the complaint before the police.

Based on such complaint,
Karkala Rural Police registered first information report in Crime No.91/2011 of their police station.
On conducting the investigation, the said police filed charge sheet against respondent No.1 for the offences punishable under Sections 279, 285 and 304A of IPC.

On taking cognizance of the offences,
respondent No.1 was prosecuted in C.C.No.124/2012 on the file of the II Additional Civil Judge &
JMFC, Karkala and acquitted.

sentences.text: Krishna Bhat the alleged employer of Keerthi apparently claiming that the accident occurred during the course of employment and compensation from the said respondents.
Ex. P8
the certified copy of the order sheet in ECA No.53/2014 shows that on 23.04.2016 the claimants filed memo for dismissal of the said petition as not pressed.
The said Court dismissed the said petition as not pressed.

6. On 30.07.2016, the claimants filed M.V.C.No.365/2016 against the driver, owner and the insurer of the Lorry No.KA-53-5298 claiming compensation of Rs.20,00,000/- on the ground that the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1.
They claimed that they were all dependents on the deceased and due to his death they have suffered damages and the respondents are liable to pay the said compensation to them.
The claimants contend that the deceased was working as Operator in JCB under one Anantha Krishna Bhat and earning more than Rs.10,000/- per month.
7. Respondent No.1 did not contest the petition.
Respondent Nos.2 and 3 alone contested the claim petition denying actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1, age, occupation, income of the deceased.

Respondent No.2 contended that the vehicle was insured with respondent No.3,
therefore if at all any compensation is awarded, respondent No.3 is liable to indemnify the same.

Respondent No.3 denied the alleged employment of the deceased under Anantha Krishna Bhat and contended that the deceased was travelling in the insured vehicle as unauthorized passenger,
thereby there is breach of policy condition and it is not liable to pay the compensation.
8. To substantiate their claim, the claimants examined claimant No.1 as PW.1 and the complainant in the criminal case as PW.2 and got marked Exs.P1 to P8.
On behalf of respondent No.3 its Officer was examined as RW.1 and Exs.R1 to R2 were marked.
9. The Tribunal on hearing the parties by the impugned award held that, the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of the driver of the lorry.
The Tribunal relying on the evidence of PW.2 and Exs.P1 to P7 held that the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1.

The Tribunal considered the income of the deceased notionally at Rs.10,000/- per month, added 40% of the same by way of future prospects, deducted 1/4th in the income for personal and living expenses of the deceased, applied 15 multiplier and awarded compensation of Rs.18,90,000/- on the head of loss of dependency.

11.

The Tribunal further held that the deceased was travelling in the lorry as unauthorized passenger, therefore insurer is not liable to indemnify the damages and dismissed the petition against the insurer.
The Tribunal allowed the petition only against respondent Nos.1 and 2 i.e. the driver and the owner of the offending vehicle.
12. The claimants, the registered owner and the driver of the vehicle challenge the award on the ground that exonerating the insurer is contrary to the evidence on record and law on point.
The registered owner and the driver of the vehicle challenge the award on the ground of negligence and quantum also.

Submissions of Sri P.P.Hegde, learned Senior Counsel appearing for Sri Sandesh T.B., learned Counsel on record for the owner and the driver:
13.
The complaint and other evidence on record show that the deceased was travelling as the representative of the owner of JCB.

Therefore under Section 147(1)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act,
1988 (for short 'MV Act') the policy covers his risk also.
Even otherwise the evidence on record shows that the deceased suffered electrocution when he had almost alighted from the lorry and touched the ground.
Therefore he becomes third party.
The policy was comprehensive policy.
Therefore the insurer is liable to indemnify the damages.
To cover the risk of the owner of the goods and representative of the owner of the goods, separate premium need not be paid as they are statutorily covered.
Even otherwise as per the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the insurer is liable to pay and recover the same from the owner of the vehicle.
The quantum of compensation awarded is on the higher side.

14. In support of his submissions, he relies upon the following judgments:
(i) National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Sarojamma and Ors.1 (ii) National Insurance Co. Ld. v. Baljit Kaur2 (iii) Anu Bhanvara v. Iffco Tokio General Insurance Co. Ltd.3 (iv) New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Yallavva and Another4 ILR 2008 KAR 542 (2004) 2 SCC 1 (2020) 20 SCC 632 ILR 2020 KAR 2239

Submissions of Sri Harsha G, learned Counsel for the claimants:
15.

So for as exoneration of the insurer, he adopts the arguments of Sri P.P.Hedge, learned Senior Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170586134/
6 Counsel.

entities.text: Senior Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The notional income considered by the Tribunal is on the lower side and the applicable multiplier is 16.
Therefore, 15 multiplier applied by the Tribunal is erroneous.
The compensation awarded on all the heads is on the lower side.

Submissions of Sri O.Mahesh, learned Counsel for the Insurer:
16.

According to the claimants, the deceased was working as Operator in JCB under one Anantha Krishna Bhat and he was travelling in the lorry by sitting in the JCB as representative of the owner of the JCB.
To prove the same they did not choose to examine the said employer.
The fact that they withdrew ECA No.53/2014 further negated their claim that he was employed in JCB.
PW.1 was not an eyewitness to the incident.
PW.2 being inmate of the lorry and eyewitness itself is doubtful.
The theory of the victim suffering electrocution while he was alighting from the lorry is apparently manipulation and contrary to the evidence on record.
Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the insurer.
Section 147(5) of the MV Act does not apply.
The deceased was unauthorized passenger.

17. Having regard to the submissions of learned counsels and on considering the materials on record, the questions that arise for consideration of this Court are:
(i) Whether the finding of the Tribunal that the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of the driver of the lorry is sustainable?
(ii) Whether the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the Insurer?
(iii) Whether the compensation awarded is just one?

Reg. Point Nos.1 and 2:
18.
According to the claimants, the deceased was employed under one Anantha Krishna Bhat to work as Operator in JCB bearing No.JS-81.
His employer had hired insured lorry for transportation of JCB to Kanthavara village.
Accordingly JCB was loaded in the lorry.
It is their case that on the instructions of his employer, he was travelling in the lorry by sitting in the cabin of the loaded JCB.
Therefore the risk of the deceased was covered as the person travelling in the lorry as a representative of the owner of the goods as contemplated under Section 147(1)(b)(i) of the MV Act.
Therefore, it was contended that the Insurer was liable to indemnify the damages.
19. To claim the benefit of Section 147(1)(b)(i) of the MV Act, the requirements of the said provision has to be satisfied.

Therefore, it is useful to extract Section 147(1)(b)(i) of the MV Act which reads as follows:
"147 Requirements of policies and limits of liability.--(1) In order to comply with the requirements of this Chapter, a policy of insurance must be a policy which--

(a) .........................................................................................
Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170586134/
7 (b) insures the person or classes of persons specified in the policy to the extent specified in sub-section (2)--
(i) against any liability which may be incurred by him in respect of the death of or bodily injury to any person, including owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the vehicle or damage to any property of a third party caused by or arising out of the use of the vehicle in a public place;
(ii) against the death of or bodily injury to any passenger of a public service vehicle caused by or arising out of the use of the vehicle in a public place:"
20 . It is no doubt true that the insurer does not dispute that the policy issued in respect of the offending lorry was in force at the time of the accident.
Ex.R2 is the said policy.

But to succeed in such contention, the appellants in both these cases should have established the basic fact of Anantha Krishna Bhat being the owner of the JCB and he employing deceased Keerthi in the JCB as the operator and deceased travelling in the lorry as his representative.
21. It is material to note that respondent No.1 the driver of the lorry did not contest the petition at all before the Tribunal.
Without contesting the petition, now he has joined the owner of the insured lorry in filing the appeal.
Neither the claimants nor respondent Nos.1 and 2 examined said Anantha Krishna Bhat to substantiate the above said contention.
Absolutely there was no explanation for non examination of Anantha Krishna Bhat.
Contrary to such case of the claimants, PW.1 in her cross-examination states that her husband Keerthi was working as JCB Operator under respondent No.1 (the driver of the lorry) since two years.
Again she says that her husband was working in Karkala under respondent No.2 (the owner of the lorry).
Such unequivocal admissions of PW.1 are further fortified by the claimants' own document Ex.P8 the copy of the order sheet in ECA No.53/2014.
If Anantha Krishna Bhat was the employer of the deceased Keerthi, then the said application should have been filed only against him.
But in that case, they impleaded the owner of the lorry as respondent No.1.
To explain that even the copy of the application in ECA No.53/2014 is not produced.

22. The evidence of PW.2 the alleged Assistant Operator of JCB was attempted to be relied on, to further contend that the deceased was travelling in the lorry as the representative of the owner of the goods.
PW.2 claims that he was the Assistant Operator in the JCB, when himself and the deceased were travelling in the lorry, he witnessed the incident and filed the complaint.
But PW.1's evidence that her husband was working under PW.2 as Operator of JCB and her brother- in-law Gopal filed the complaint belies his evidence.
It is also to be noted that Ex.P1 contains several corrections and interpolations.

Such unequivocal admissions of PW.1 and Ex.P8 demolish the case of the claimants and the other appellants herein that Keerthi was travelling in the lorry along with JCB as the representative of the owner of JCB.
23.
Ex . R2
the Insurance Policy shows that the seating capacity of the lorry was three.
The vehicle in question was a goods vehicle.
If at all any one has to travel in the said lorry, they have to travel sitting in the cabin of the lorry and not in the body of the lorry.

Since the fact of the deceased Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170586134/
8 travelling as the representative of the owner of the goods itself was not proved, the judgment in Sarojamma's case referred to supra relied upon by learned Senior Counsel is not applicable.

sentences.text:
In Baljit Kaur's case and in Anu Bhanwara's case referred to supra relied on by the learned Senior Counsel,
the order of pay and recover was passed exercising the power under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.
Therefore, the said judgments do not advance the case of the driver and owner of the insured vehicle.
Under the aforesaid facts and circumstances, the Tribunal's finding that the deceased was travelling as an unauthorized passenger in the lorry does not warrant any interference.
24. So far as the rashness and negligence and the manner of the occurrence of the accident the claimants did not produce the charge sheet copies.
As already pointed out, PW.1 being the eyewitness is doubtful.
According to PW.2 and the complaint version, respondent No.1 drove the lorry in rash and negligent manner.
Consequently the lorry came in contact with live electric wire which was passing over the road.
It is further contended that on seeing that the deceased was trying to alight from the lorry, when he kept his foot on the ground, he got electrocuted and died.
Both these facts were denied by the owner and insurer of the lorry in their statement of objections.

25. According to PW.2 after sighting the lorry coming in contact with the live electric wire, the driver stopped the lorry, then PW.2 first alighted from the lorry, followed by Keerthi, when Keerthi's feet touched the ground, he was electrocuted.
In the ordinary course, if the live wire comes in contact with the JCB or the lorry, the inmates of the same should get electrocuted there only.
If the electricity enters Keerthi through his feet from the ground, then the same should have happened to PW.2 who had alighted from the lorry first.
26. To accept PW.2's contention, there should be evidence to show that the electricity entered Keerthi through his feet.
But the claimants' own document Ex.P5 the postmortem report states that entry point of the current was right little finger of the deceased and exit point was second and third toe of right foot.
Ex. P5

further shows that the burn injuries were found in right hand fingers, nose,
abdomen and chest.
P4 the spot mahazar states that on either side of the road, there were shrubs and grass and the electric wire had touched the JCB.
That does not indicate that the wire had cut and fallen on the vehicles or on the ground.

Since entry point of current was right little finger the only probable inference applying res ipsa loquitur principle is that the deceased might have tried to handle the live electric wire and suffered the injuries.

When PW.1 says that her husband was working with PW.2 since two years as JCB Operator, PW.2 in his cross-examination states that he knew the deceased only since four months prior to the incident and he was not his relative.
In the light of the above said facts and circumstances, the evidence of PW.2 regarding the manner of occurrence of the accident does not inspire the confidence of the Court.

28. Despite the above referred inconsistencies and embellishments in the evidence of the claimants,
still the fact of respondent No.1 carrying the JCB in the lorry with the deceased in the cabin of the loaded JCB and the deceased suffering electrocution in the cabin of the loaded JCB were not disputed and stood proved.
That was an actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1 for which respondent No.2 is vicariously liable.

By so travelling in the lorry sitting in the cabin of the Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/170586134/
9 loaded JCB and handling the live wire, the deceased also equally contributed to the accident and the consequential death.

entities.text: Smt Veena Kumari vs Mahesh Rao
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, both of them are guilty of negligence equally.

29. The Tribunal without appreciating all the aforesaid facts, just referring to the evidence of PW.2 and the exhibits, without analyzing the same reached the erroneous conclusion as to the negligence.

Despite respondent No.3 examining RW.1, the Tribunal while discussing the issue of negligence says that the respondents have not led oral evidence and has not disproved the documentary evidence of the claimants.

The Tribunal has failed to examine the documents produced by the claimants meaningfully which falsified the case of the claimants regarding the manner of occurrence of the accident, more particularly the version of PW.2 when the basic burden of proving the said fact was not discharged by the claimants, there would not have been any question of the respondents disproving the case of the claimants.
Therefore, the finding of the Tribunal regarding rashness and negligence requires to be modified fastening 50% negligence to the deceased himself.

Reg. 
Quantum:
30.
Then the question is whether the quantum of compensation is just one.
As per the postmortem report the deceased was aged 31 years.
Though the claimants contend that he was earning more than Rs.10,000/- per month, no evidence was adduced in proof of actual income.
The accident occurred in the year 2011.
There was no material to show that the deceased had any training in operating the JCB or he was skilled labour.
Having regard to the age of the deceased, wage rates and the cost of living prevailing during the year 2011, income at Rs.10,000/- per month considered by the Tribunal is on the higher side.
For the said period, this Court consistently considered the wage of the unskilled labour for the year 2011 at Rs.6,500/- per month.

31. In the light of the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Company Limited vs. Pranay Sethi5 and having regard to the age and employment of the deceased, future prospects at the rate of 40% of his income has to be super added to the income.

entities.text: National Insurance Company Limited vs. Pranay Sethi5
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, his monthly income comes to Rs.6,500/- + 2,600= Rs.9,100/-.
The deceased had four dependants.
As per the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sarla Varma v. Delhi Transport th Corporation6 1/4 of the income has to be deducted for his personal and living expenses.

entities.text: Sarla Varma v. Delhi Transport th Corporation6
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, his net income comes to Rs.6,825/- and the applicable multiplier is 16.
Therefore, the compensation payable under the head of loss of dependency comes to Rs.6,825 X 16 X 12 = Rs.13,10,400/-.

As per the AIR 2017 SC 5157 AIR 2009 SC 3104 judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pranay Sethi's case and Magma General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Nanu Ram7 each of the claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.40,000/- with escalation at 10% on the head of loss of consortium which comes to Rs.44,000/- X 4 =Rs.1,76,000/-.
32.

entities.text: Magma General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Nanu Ram7
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Similarly, the claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.15,000/- on the head of loss of estate and Rs.15,000/- on the head of funeral expenses and transportation with escalation at 10% which comes to Rs.33,000/-.
Therefore, the just compensation payable is Rs.14,89,700/-.

10  2 Loss of consortium 1,76,000/-

33.

Since the deceased had also contributed to 50% of the negligence in the occurrence of the accident and his death, the claimants are entitled to compensation of 50% out of Rs.15,19,400/-
which comes to Rs.7,59,700/- with interest thereon at 6% per annum.
In the light of the above 2018 (18) SCC 130 observation, dismissal of the claim petition against insurer needs to be confirmed.
Respondent Nos.1 and 2 i.e. the driver and owner of the lorry are jointly and severally liable to pay the aforesaid compensation to the claimants.
Therefore, the appeals deserve to be allowed in part.

Hence the following:
ORDER
The appeals are partly allowed.
The impugned award is modified as follows:
(i) The claim petition against respondent No.3 Insurer is dismissed.
(ii) The claim petition against respondent Nos.1 and 2 is partly allowed.
(iii) The claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.7,59,700/- with interest thereon at 6% per annum from the date of petition till its realization.
(iv) Respondent Nos.1 and 2 shall deposit the said amount before the Tribunal, on adjusting the compensation already deposited if any within four weeks from the date of receipt of copy of this order.
(v) Out of the compensation so deposited, claimant Nos.1 to 3 are entitled to receive share of 30% each and claimant No.4 is entitled to receive 10% share.
(vi) The share of claimant Nos.1 and 4 shall be released to them.

THESE MISCELLANEOUS FIRST APPEALS HAVING BEEN HEARD AND RESERVED ON 30.03.2023 COMING ON FOR PRONOUNCEMENT OF JUDGMENT THIS DAY, K.S.MUDAGAL J.,
DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 JUDGMENT Challenging the award in M.V.C.No.365/2016 on the file of the Senior Civil Judge and MACT,
Mudigere, the claimants have preferred M.F.A.No.1839/2018 and the registered owner and the driver of the insured vehicle have preferred M.F.A.No.2818/2018.
2.
opennyai_summary.facts:
6. On 30.07.2016, the claimants filed M.V.C.No.365/2016 against the driver, owner and the insurer of the Lorry No.KA-53-5298 claiming compensation of Rs.20,00,000/- on the ground that the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1.
They claimed that they were all dependents on the deceased and due to his death they have suffered damages and the respondents are liable to pay the said compensation to them.
The claimants contend that the deceased was working as Operator in JCB under one Anantha Krishna Bhat and earning more than Rs.10,000/- per month.
Respondent Nos.2 and 3 alone contested the claim petition denying actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1, age, occupation, income of the deceased.
Respondent No.3 denied the alleged employment of the deceased under Anantha Krishna Bhat and contended that the deceased was travelling in the insured vehicle as unauthorized passenger,
thereby there is breach of policy condition and it is not liable to pay the compensation.
9. The Tribunal on hearing the parties by the impugned award held that, the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of the driver of the lorry.
Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the insurer.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
12. The claimants, the registered owner and the driver of the vehicle challenge the award on the ground that exonerating the insurer is contrary to the evidence on record and law on point.
The registered owner and the driver of the vehicle challenge the award on the ground of negligence and quantum also.
The complaint and other evidence on record show that the deceased was travelling as the representative of the owner of JCB.
Therefore under Section 147(1)(b) of the Motor Vehicles Act,
1988 (for short 'MV Act') the policy covers his risk also.
Even otherwise the evidence on record shows that the deceased suffered electrocution when he had almost alighted from the lorry and touched the ground.
Therefore he becomes third party.
The policy was comprehensive policy.
Therefore the insurer is liable to indemnify the damages.
To cover the risk of the owner of the goods and representative of the owner of the goods, separate premium need not be paid as they are statutorily covered.
Even otherwise as per the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the insurer is liable to pay and recover the same from the owner of the vehicle.
The quantum of compensation awarded is on the higher side.
14. In support of his submissions, he relies upon the following judgments:
(i) National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Sarojamma and Ors.1 (ii) National Insurance Co. Ld. v. Baljit Kaur2 (iii) Anu Bhanvara v. Iffco Tokio General Insurance Co. Ltd.3 (iv) New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Yallavva and Another4 ILR 2008 KAR 542 (2004) 2 SCC 1 (2020) 20 SCC 632 ILR 2020 KAR 2239
PW.1 was not an eyewitness to the incident.
The theory of the victim suffering electrocution while he was alighting from the lorry is apparently manipulation and contrary to the evidence on record.
Section 147(5) of the MV Act does not apply.
opennyai_summary.issue:
The deceased was unauthorized passenger.
17. Having regard to the submissions of learned counsels and on considering the materials on record, the questions that arise for consideration of this Court are:
(i) Whether the finding of the Tribunal that the accident occurred due to actionable negligence on the part of the driver of the lorry is sustainable?
(ii) Whether the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the Insurer?
(iii) Whether the compensation awarded is just one?
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Therefore the risk of the deceased was covered as the person travelling in the lorry as a representative of the owner of the goods as contemplated under Section 147(1)(b)(i) of the MV Act.
That was an actionable negligence on the part of respondent No.1 for which respondent No.2 is vicariously liable.
The Tribunal has failed to examine the documents produced by the claimants meaningfully which falsified the case of the claimants regarding the manner of occurrence of the accident, more particularly the version of PW.2 when the basic burden of proving the said fact was not discharged by the claimants, there would not have been any question of the respondents disproving the case of the claimants.
As per the AIR 2017 SC 5157 AIR 2009 SC 3104 judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pranay Sethi's case and Magma General Insurance Company Ltd. v. Nanu Ram7 each of the claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.40,000/- with escalation at 10% on the head of loss of consortium which comes to Rs.44,000/- X 4 =Rs.1,76,000/-.
32.
opennyai_summary.decision:
The deceased had four dependants.
Therefore, the compensation payable under the head of loss of dependency comes to Rs.6,825 X 16 X 12 = Rs.13,10,400/-.
Similarly, the claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.15,000/- on the head of loss of estate and Rs.15,000/- on the head of funeral expenses and transportation with escalation at 10% which comes to Rs.33,000/-.
Therefore, the just compensation payable is Rs.14,89,700/-.
Sl. Particulars Compensation  No. amount in Rs.
 1 Loss of dependency 13,10,400/-
Since the deceased had also contributed to 50% of the negligence in the occurrence of the accident and his death, the claimants are entitled to compensation of 50% out of Rs.15,19,400/-
which comes to Rs.7,59,700/- with interest thereon at 6% per annum.
In the light of the above 2018 (18) SCC 130 observation, dismissal of the claim petition against insurer needs to be confirmed.
Respondent Nos.1 and 2 i.e. the driver and owner of the lorry are jointly and severally liable to pay the aforesaid compensation to the claimants.
Therefore, the appeals deserve to be allowed in part.
Hence the following:
ORDER
The appeals are partly allowed.
The impugned award is modified as follows:
(i) The claim petition against respondent No.3 Insurer is dismissed.
(ii) The claim petition against respondent Nos.1 and 2 is partly allowed.
(iii) The claimants are entitled to compensation of Rs.7,59,700/- with interest thereon at 6% per annum from the date of petition till its realization.
(iv) Respondent Nos.1 and 2 shall deposit the said amount before the Tribunal, on adjusting the compensation already deposited if any within four weeks from the date of receipt of copy of this order.
(v) Out of the compensation so deposited, claimant Nos.1 to 3 are entitled to receive share of 30% each and claimant No.4 is entitled to receive 10% share.
(vi) The share of claimant Nos.1 and 4 shall be released to them.
The share of c l a i m a n t N o s . 2 a n d 3 s h a l l b e i n v e s t e d i n F i x e d D e p o s i t i n a n y Nationalized/Scheduled Bank of the choice of claimant No.1 till they attain majority with liberty to claimant No.1 to draw the accrued interest on such deposit.
(vii) Registry shall transmit the amount in deposit if any and trial Court records to the Tribunal forthwith.
